question: According to the essay, what were the two main limitations Paul Graham faced when trying to write programs on the IBM 1401 computer in 9th grade, and how did these limitations affect what he could accomplish?
answer:
# Two Main Limitations on the IBM 1401

According to the essay, the two main limitations Paul Graham faced were:

1. **Limited input options**: The only form of input to programs was data stored on punched cards, and he didn't have any data stored on punched cards.

2. **Limited mathematical knowledge**: The only alternative was to do things that didn't rely on input (like calculate approximations of pi), but he didn't know enough math to do anything interesting of that type.

**Effect on accomplishment**: These limitations meant he couldn't write programs that did much of anything. He can't even remember any programs he wrote because they were so limited in scope. His clearest memory is actually of writing a program that didn't terminate, which caused a social error at the data center.
contexts:
What I Worked On

February 2021

Before college the two main things I worked on, outside of school, were writing and programming. I didn't write essays. I wrote what beginning writers were supposed to write then, and probably still are: short stories. My stories were awful. They had hardly any plot, just characters with strong feelings, which I imagined made them deep.

The first programs I tried writing were on the IBM 1401 that our school district used for what was then called "data processing." This was in 9th grade, so I was 13 or 14. The school district's 1401 happened to be in the basement of our junior high school, and my friend Rich Draves and I got permission to use it. It was like a mini Bond villain's lair down there, with all these alien-looking machines — CPU, disk drives, printer, card reader — sitting up on a raised floor under bright fluorescent lights.

The language we used was an early version of Fortran. You had to type programs on punch cards, then stack them in the card reader and press a button to load the program into memory and run it. The result would ordinarily be to print something on the spectacularly loud printer.

I was puzzled by the 1401. I couldn't figure out what to do with it. And in retrospect there's not much I could have done with it. The only form of input to programs was data stored on punched cards, and I didn't have any data stored on punched cards. The only other option was to do things that didn't rely on any input, like calculate approximations of pi, but I didn't know enough math to do anything interesting of that type. So I'm not surprised I can't remember any programs I wrote, because they can't have done much. My clearest memory is of the moment I learned it was possible for programs not to terminate, when one of mine didn't. On a machine without time-sharing, this was a social as well as a technical error, as the data center manager's expression made clear.

With microcomputers, everything changed. Now you could have a computer sitting right in front of you, on a desk, that could respond to your keystrokes as it was running instead of just churning through a stack of punch cards and then stopping. [1]

The first of my friends to get a microcomputer built it himself. It was sold as a kit by Heathkit. I remember vividly how impressed and envious I felt watching him sitting in front of it, typing programs right into the computer.

Computer Science is an uneasy alliance between two halves, theory and systems. The theory people prove things, and the systems people build things. I wanted to build things. I had plenty of respect for theory — indeed, a sneaking suspicion that it was the more admirable of the two halves — but building things seemed so much more exciting.

The problem with systems work, though, was that it didn't last. Any program you wrote today, no matter how good, would be obsolete in a couple decades at best. People might mention your software in footnotes, but no one would actually use it. And indeed, it would seem very feeble work. Only people with a sense of the history of the field would even realize that, in its time, it had been good.

There were some surplus Xerox Dandelions floating around the computer lab at one point. Anyone who wanted one to play around with could have one. I was briefly tempted, but they were so slow by present standards; what was the point? No one else wanted one either, so off they went. That was what happened to systems work.

I wanted not just to build things, but to build things that would last.

question: Paul Graham initially planned to study philosophy in college but eventually switched to AI. Explain his reasoning for this decision based on what he discovered about philosophy as a field of study.
answer:
# Paul Graham's Decision to Switch from Philosophy to AI

Based on the context, Paul Graham switched from philosophy to AI because he discovered that philosophy as a field of study was fundamentally limited and uninteresting.

Specifically, he found that:

1. **Other fields occupied the intellectual space**: Other academic disciplines took up so much of the space of ideas that there was little room left for philosophy's supposed "ultimate truths."

2. **Philosophy was relegated to edge cases**: What remained for philosophy were only "edge cases that people in other fields felt could safely be ignored"—rather than the powerful study of ultimate truths he had envisioned.

3. **The courses were boring**: When he actually took philosophy courses in college, he found them consistently dull and uninspiring.

Rather than articulating these disappointments explicitly, Graham simply experienced repeated boredom in philosophy courses, which prompted him to switch to AI as an alternative field of study.
contexts:
Computers were expensive in those days and it took me years of nagging before I convinced my father to buy one, a TRS-80, in about 1980. The gold standard then was the Apple II, but a TRS-80 was good enough. This was when I really started programming. I wrote simple games, a program to predict how high my model rockets would fly, and a word processor that my father used to write at least one book. There was only room in memory for about 2 pages of text, so he'd write 2 pages at a time and then print them out, but it was a lot better than a typewriter.

Though I liked programming, I didn't plan to study it in college. In college I was going to study philosophy, which sounded much more powerful. It seemed, to my naive high school self, to be the study of the ultimate truths, compared to which the things studied in other fields would be mere domain knowledge. What I discovered when I got to college was that the other fields took up so much of the space of ideas that there wasn't much left for these supposed ultimate truths. All that seemed left for philosophy were edge cases that people in other fields felt could safely be ignored.

I couldn't have put this into words when I was 18. All I knew at the time was that I kept taking philosophy courses and they kept being boring. So I decided to switch to AI.

What these programs really showed was that there's a subset of natural language that's a formal language. But a very proper subset. It was clear that there was an unbridgeable gap between what they could do and actually understanding natural language. It was not, in fact, simply a matter of teaching SHRDLU more words. That whole way of doing AI, with explicit data structures representing concepts, was not going to work. Its brokenness did, as so often happens, generate a lot of opportunities to write papers about various band-aids that could be applied to it, but it was never going to get us Mike.

So I looked around to see what I could salvage from the wreckage of my plans, and there was Lisp. I knew from experience that Lisp was interesting for its own sake and not just for its association with AI, even though that was the main reason people cared about it at the time. So I decided to focus on Lisp. In fact, I decided to write a book about Lisp hacking. It's scary to think how little I knew about Lisp hacking when I started writing that book. But there's nothing like writing a book about something to help you learn it. The book, On Lisp, wasn't published till 1993, but I wrote much of it in grad school.

# Paul Graham's Reasoning for Switching from Philosophy to AI

Based on the essay, Paul Graham's decision to switch from philosophy to AI was driven by his disappointing discovery about what philosophy actually offered as a field of study.

## His Initial Expectations vs. Reality

Graham initially believed philosophy was "the study of the ultimate truths, compared to which the things studied in other fields would be mere domain knowledge." However, when he arrived at college, he discovered this was not the case.

## What He Found Instead

He discovered that **other fields took up so much of the space of ideas that there wasn't much left for these supposed ultimate truths.** As he puts it: "All that seemed left for philosophy were edge cases that people in other fields felt could safely be ignored."

In other words, philosophy had been reduced to addressing only the peripheral questions and problems that other disciplines didn't consider important enough to tackle.

## The Practical Outcome

Rather than continue with a field that felt intellectually limiting, Graham made a pragmatic decision: "I kept taking philosophy courses and they kept being boring. So I decided to switch to AI."

His switch to AI was motivated by two specific inspirations: a Heinlein novel featuring an intelligent computer and a PBS documentary demonstrating Terry Winograd's SHRDLU program—both of which made AI seem like an exciting and imminent frontier.

question: Paul Graham initially pursued AI in graduate school but eventually realized that the AI approaches being practiced at the time were fundamentally flawed. Explain what Graham identified as the core problem with the AI methods of that era, and describe how this realization led him to change his academic focus.
answer:
# Graham's Critique of AI and His Pivot

## The Core Problem

Graham identified that the AI methods of his era were fundamentally limited in their approach to natural language understanding. Specifically, he realized that programs like SHRDLU—which converted natural language statements into formal representations and stored them as "knowledge"—were only working with "a subset of natural language that's a formal language. But a very proper subset."

The critical flaw was that **there was an unbridgeable gap between what these programs could do and actually understanding natural language**. Graham emphasized that this wasn't a problem that could be solved by simply teaching the programs more words or refining the approach—the entire methodology of using explicit data structures to represent concepts was fundamentally broken and would never achieve genuine language understanding.

## His Shift in Focus

Rather than pursuing AI further, Graham "looked around to see what I could salvage from the wreckage of my plans." He discovered that **Lisp itself was intellectually interesting independent of its AI applications**, even though AI had been the main reason people cared about it.

Consequently, he **redirected his academic focus to Lisp**, deciding to write a book about Lisp hacking (which became *On Lisp*, published in 1993). He wrote much of this book during his graduate school years.

At the time this bothered me, but now it seems amusingly accurate, for reasons I was about to discover.

I applied to 3 grad schools: MIT and Yale, which were renowned for AI at the time, and Harvard, which I'd visited because Rich Draves went there, and was also home to Bill Woods, who'd invented the type of parser I used in my SHRDLU clone. Only Harvard accepted me, so that was where I went.

I don't remember the moment it happened, or if there even was a specific moment, but during the first year of grad school I realized that AI, as practiced at the time, was a hoax. By which I mean the sort of AI in which a program that's told "the dog is sitting on the chair" translates this into some formal representation and adds it to the list of things it knows.

I knew from experience that Lisp was interesting for its own sake and not just for its association with AI, even though that was the main reason people cared about it at the time. But there's nothing like writing a book about something to help you learn it. The book, On Lisp, wasn't published till 1993, but I wrote much of it in grad school.

McCarthy's 1960 Lisp did nothing more than interpret Lisp expressions. It was missing a lot of things you'd want in a programming language. So these had to be added, and when they were, they weren't defined using McCarthy's original axiomatic approach. That wouldn't have been feasible at the time. McCarthy tested his interpreter by hand-simulating the execution of programs. But it was already getting close to the limit of interpreters you could test that way — indeed, there was a bug in it that McCarthy had overlooked. To test a more complicated interpreter, you'd have had to run it, and computers then weren't powerful enough.

Now they are, though. Now you could continue using McCarthy's axiomatic approach till you'd defined a complete programming language. And as long as every change you made to McCarthy's Lisp was a discoveredness-preserving transformation, you could, in principle, end up with a complete language that had this quality. Harder to do than to talk about, of course, but if it was possible in principle, why not try? So I decided to take a shot at it. It took 4 years, from March 26, 2015 to October 12, 2019. It was fortunate that I had a precisely defined goal, or it would have been hard to keep at it for so long.

## The Core Problem with AI Methods

Graham identified that the fundamental flaw in AI approaches of that era was their reliance on **explicit data structures representing concepts**. Specifically, he realized that programs which translated natural language statements (like "the dog is sitting on the chair") into formal representations and stored them as knowledge were based on a flawed premise.

According to the essay, Graham's two specific inspirations to work on AI in the mid-1980s were:

1. **A novel by Robert Heinlein** called *The Moon is a Harsh Mistress*, which featured an intelligent computer named Mike
2. **A PBS documentary** showing Terry Winograd using SHRDLU

# Why He Learned Lisp and Its Impact

Graham decided to focus on Lisp after recognizing that the SHRDLU approach to AI was fundamentally flawed. He realized there was "an unbridgeable gap between what they could do and actually understanding natural language," and that explicit data structures representing concepts "was not going to work."

Knowing from experience that Lisp was "interesting for its own sake," he decided to write a book about Lisp hacking (*On Lisp*, published in 1993).

Regarding Lisp's impact on his understanding: The essay indicates that Lisp's distinctive nature—its core being a language defined by writing an interpreter in itself, combined with its origins as a formal model of computation rather than an ordinary programming language—gave it "a power and elegance that other languages couldn't match." This is what attracted Graham in college, though he didn't fully understand why at the time.

question: Paul Graham mentions that he was dissatisfied with systems work in computer science because programs become obsolete quickly. What realization did he have while visiting the Carnegie Institute in 1988, and how did this realization influence his career decisions at that time?
answer:
# Paul Graham's Realization at the Carnegie Institute

While looking at a painting at the Carnegie Institute in 1988, Paul Graham realized that **paintings don't become obsolete** — some of the best ones were hundreds of years old. This contrasted sharply with software, which he saw as temporary and destined to fade into obscurity.

This realization influenced him to consider **becoming a painter**. He recognized that:

1. Art was something that could last, unlike software
2. It was possible to make a living as an artist (though not as easily as through software)
3. Artists could be truly independent — without a boss or need for research funding

Though Graham admitted he had never imagined actually being able to make art himself, this moment prompted him to seriously consider whether he could pursue painting as a career path that would create work of lasting value.

question: Describe the situation Paul Graham found himself in during his PhD program at Harvard. What were the multiple projects he was working on simultaneously, and how did he eventually resolve his dilemma about completing his degree?
answer:
# Paul Graham's PhD Dilemma at Harvard

During his PhD program in computer science at Harvard, Paul Graham found himself in a conflicting situation:

**Multiple Projects:**
- Pursuing a PhD in computer science (his official program)
- Taking art classes in various departments
- Working on a programming project called "On Lisp" and Lisp hacking, which he was genuinely passionate about
- Planning to become an artist

**The Resolution:**
In April 1990, his advisor Tom Cheatham unexpectedly asked if he was far enough along to graduate in June. Despite having written nothing of his dissertation, Graham made a quick decision to attempt writing it in the remaining 5 weeks. He planned to reuse parts of his "On Lisp" work where possible. He agreed to provide something for Cheatham to read within a few days, and successfully completed his degree that June.

Graham notes that he "didn't see a way out" of the situation—he didn't want to drop out, but his energies were directed toward projects other than his thesis. His advisor's question ultimately forced a resolution that allowed him to graduate while leveraging the work he had already done.

I didn't see a way out of this situation. I didn't want to drop out of grad school, but how else was I going to get out? I remember when my friend Robert Morris got kicked out of Cornell for writing the internet worm of 1988, I was envious that he'd found such a spectacular way to get out of grad school.

Then one day in April 1990 a crack appeared in the wall. I ran into professor Cheatham and he asked if I was far enough along to graduate that June. I didn't have a word of my dissertation written, but in what must have been the quickest bit of thinking in my life, I decided to take a shot at writing one in the 5 weeks or so that remained before the deadline, reusing parts of On Lisp where I could, and I was able to respond, with no perceptible delay "Yes, I think so. I wrote this new Lisp, called Bel, in itself in Arc. That may sound like a contradiction, but it's an indication of the sort of trickery I had to engage in to make this work. By means of an egregious collection of hacks I managed to make something close enough to an interpreter written in itself that could actually run. Not fast, but fast enough to test.

I had to ban myself from writing essays during most of this time, or I'd never have finished. In late 2015 I spent 3 months writing essays, and when I went back to working on Bel I could barely understand the code. Not so much because it was badly written as because the problem is so convoluted. When you're working on an interpreter written in itself, it's hard to keep track of what's happening at what level, and errors can be practically encrypted by the time you get them.

So I said no more essays till Bel was done. But I told few people about Bel while I was working on it. So for years it must have seemed that I was doing nothing, when in fact I was working harder than I'd ever worked on anything. Occasionally after wrestling for hours with some gruesome bug I'd check Twitter or HN and see someone asking "Does Paul Graham still code?"

1. **Writing a book about Lisp hacking** - He was working on "On Lisp," which he was genuinely passionate about and which would eventually be published in 1993.

2. **Taking art classes** - He had started taking art classes at Harvard in the fall, inspired by a realization that paintings could last and that one could make a living as an artist.

3. **His PhD dissertation** - Though this was nominally his primary focus, he had not actually started writing it.

## The Dilemma

Graham found himself in an uncomfortable position: he didn't want to drop out of grad school, but he was deeply invested in these other pursuits rather than his dissertation work. He even expressed envy when his friend Robert Morris got kicked out of Cornell, viewing it as a "spectacular way to get out of grad school."

## The Resolution

The breakthrough came in April 1990 when Professor Tom Cheatham (his advisor) asked if he was far enough along to graduate that June. Despite having not written a single word of his dissertation, Graham made a quick decision to attempt writing one in the remaining 5 weeks. He reused parts of "On Lisp" where possible and successfully completed his dissertation in time to graduate.

**The two institutions were:**
1. RISD (Rhode Island School of Design) in the US
2. Accademia di Belli Arti in Florence

I picked applications of continuations as the topic. In retrospect I should have written about macros and embedded languages. There's a whole world there that's barely been explored. But all I wanted was to get out of grad school, and my rapidly written dissertation sufficed, just barely.

Meanwhile I was applying to art schools. I applied to two: RISD in the US, and the Accademia di Belli Arti in Florence, which, because it was the oldest art school, I imagined would be good. RISD accepted me, and I never heard back from the Accademia, so off to Providence I went.

I'd applied for the BFA program at RISD, which meant in effect that I had to go to college again. This was not as strange as it sounds, because I was only 25, and art schools are full of people of different ages. RISD counted me as a transfer sophomore and said I had to do the foundation that summer. The foundation means the classes that everyone has to take in fundamental subjects like drawing, color, and design.

Toward the end of the summer I got a big surprise: a letter from the Accademia, which had been delayed because they'd sent it to Cambridge England instead of Cambridge Massachusetts, inviting me to take the entrance exam in Florence that fall. This was now only weeks away. My nice landlady let me leave my stuff in her attic. I had some money saved from consulting work I'd done in grad school; there was probably enough to last a year if I lived cheaply. Now all I had to do was learn Italian.

When I left to go back to RISD the next fall, I arranged to do freelance work for the group that did projects for customers, and this was how I survived for the next several years. When I came back to visit for a project later on, someone told me about a new thing called HTML, which was, as he described it, a derivative of SGML. Markup language enthusiasts were an occupational hazard at Interleaf and I ignored him, but this HTML thing later became a big part of my life.

In the fall of 1992 I moved back to Providence to continue at RISD. The foundation had merely been intro stuff, and the Accademia had been a (very civilized) joke. Now I was going to see what real art school was like. But alas it was more like the Accademia than not. Better organized, certainly, and a lot more expensive, but it was now becoming clear that art school did not bear the same relationship to art that medical school bore to medicine. At least not the painting department. The textile department, which my next door neighbor belonged to, seemed to be pretty rigorous. No doubt illustration and architecture were too. question: The author describes two different approaches to painting: painting people versus painting still lives. Explain the key differences between these two approaches and why the author found still life painting particularly valuable for developing his observational skills.
answer:
# Key Differences Between Painting People and Still Lives

## Approach to Subject Matter

**Painting People:** Requires knowing how to paint a generic person first, then modifying it to match the specific individual. This is necessary because people cannot sit still for extended periods (only about 15 minutes maximum).

**Painting Still Lives:** Allows the artist to copy "pixel by pixel" directly from what they're seeing, since the subject cannot move.

## Value for Observational Skills

The author found still life painting particularly valuable because it enabled a deeper level of visual analysis. Rather than stopping at photographic accuracy through direct copying, the artist can emphasize subtle visual cues—such as color changes that indicate object edges. By consciously highlighting these details, the painter can create works that are "more realistic than photographs" in a strict information-theoretic sense, meaning they convey more accurate visual information than a mechanical reproduction.

This approach forced the author to develop keen observational skills by learning to identify and artistically emphasize the specific visual indicators that communicate spatial relationships and object boundaries to the viewer.
contexts: While I was a student at the Accademia I started painting still lives in my bedroom at night. These paintings were tiny, because the room was, and because I painted them on leftover scraps of canvas, which was all I could afford at the time. Painting still lives is different from painting people, because the subject, as its name suggests, can't move. People can't sit for more than about 15 minutes at a time, and when they do they don't sit very still. So the traditional m.o. for painting people is to know how to paint a generic person, which you then modify to match the specific person you're painting. Whereas a still life you can, if you want, copy pixel by pixel from what you're seeing. You don't want to stop there, of course, or you get merely photographic accuracy, and what makes a still life interesting is that it's been through a head. You want to emphasize the visual cues that tell you, for example, that the reason the color changes suddenly at a certain point is that it's the edge of an object. By subtly emphasizing such things you can make paintings that are more realistic than photographs not just in some metaphorical sense, but in the strict information-theoretic sense. [4]

I saw Florence at street level in every possible condition, from empty dark winter evenings to sweltering summer days when the streets were packed with tourists.

[4] You can of course paint people like still lives if you want to, and they're willing. That sort of portrait is arguably the apex of still life painting, though the long sitting does tend to produce pained expressions in the sitters.

# Key Differences Between Painting People and Still Lives

Based on the context provided, the author outlines several important distinctions:

## Painting People
- **Subject movement**: People can only sit for about 15 minutes at a time and don't sit very still
- **Approach**: The traditional method involves learning to paint a generic person, then modifying it to match the specific individual being painted
- **Flexibility**: Artists work from memory and general knowledge rather than direct observation

## Painting Still Lives
- **Subject stability**: The subject cannot move, allowing for extended, uninterrupted observation
- **Approach**: The artist can copy "pixel by pixel" from what they're seeing if desired
- **Depth**: While photographic accuracy alone is insufficient, the artist can emphasize visual cues (like color changes at object edges) to create paintings that are "more realistic than photographs" in an information-theoretic sense

## Why Still Life Was Valuable for Observational Skills

The author found still life painting particularly valuable because it forced conscious awareness of visual details that normally go unnoticed. In everyday life, the brain handles visual perception unconsciously—recognizing "a water droplet" or "a bush" without processing specific details like exact lighting or leaf positions.

However, when painting a still life, the artist must look closely and deliberately notice these details. The author emphasizes that "you can still be noticing new things after days of trying to paint something people usually take for granted," making still life an excellent vehicle for developing deep observational skills.

question: Describe the author's experience at Interleaf and explain why he characterizes himself as "a bad employee." What specific factors contributed to the friction between him and his workplace environment?
answer:
# The Author's Experience at Interleaf

## His Job and Role
The author worked at Interleaf, a software company that created document creation software. He was hired as a Lisp hacker to write code in the company's custom Lisp scripting language, which they had added to their product inspired by Emacs.

## Why He Was "A Bad Employee"

The author characterizes himself as a bad employee for several reasons:

1. **Limited Technical Understanding**: Interleaf's Lisp was built on top of C, and since he didn't know C and didn't want to learn it, he never understood most of the software.

2. **Lack of Responsibility**: He describes himself as "terribly irresponsible."

3. **Conflict Over Work Hours**: The job required showing up during conventional working hours, which he found "unnatural." This created significant friction between him and the workplace environment.

4. **Divided Attention**: Toward the end of the year, he spent much of his time secretly working on his own book project, "On Lisp," rather than focusing on his Interleaf responsibilities.

The core friction stemmed from a fundamental mismatch between the company's expectation of conventional office hours and the author's belief that such structured schedules were incompatible with his working style and productivity.

The good part was that I got paid huge amounts of money, especially by art student standards. In Florence, after paying my part of the rent, my budget for everything else had been $7 a day. I learned some useful things at Interleaf, though they were mostly about what not to do. But the most important thing I learned, and which I used in both Viaweb and Y Combinator, is that the low end eats the high end: that it's good to be the "entry level" option, even though that will be less prestigious, because if you're not, someone else will be, and will squash you against the ceiling.
